candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk XII.11 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's reply to Pilate — 'Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above' — Cyril takes as the comprehensive doctrine of divine sovereignty over even the Passion's executioners. Pilate's authority is real (not denied) but derivative (not autonomous): every act of the powerful is bounded by divine permission. 'Therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin' (continuing the verse) Cyril takes as establishing graduated responsibility within the system: the Sanhedrin who delivered Christ to Pilate bear greater responsibility than Pilate, who merely executes their judgment within the bounds of his secondary authority. This nuanced reading shapes the Tewahedo Holy Week liturgy's careful theological framing.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's words from the cross to His mother and the beloved disciple — 'Woman, behold thy son! ... Behold thy mother!' — Cyril reads at multiple levels. Literally, Christ provides for Mary's continued care after His death (the eldest son's filial obligation discharged even from the cross). Typologically, Cyril takes Mary as figure of the Church and John as figure of every disciple: in establishing John as Mary's son, Christ establishes the Church as the Mother of every believer + every believer as the Church's son. The Tewahedo Marian veneration (which is particularly developed compared to other Christian traditions) draws its theological warrant from this Cyrilline reading.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's dying word — 'It is finished' (tetelestai) — Cyril takes as the dominical declaration of completed accomplishment. The perfect tense (tetelestai — completed action with continuing result) Cyril emphasizes: the work IS finished, definitively and abidingly.
